source_refs.note: Book p. 269: 14.2.2 (a) i.i = j.j = k.k = 1, (b) i.j = j.k = k.i = 0, (c) u.v = v.u, with the i, j, k axes figure. No book errors. Table, notes, tips and mistakes are ours.

blocks.text: By applying the definition of dot product to unit vectors \(\underline{i}\), \(\underline{j}\) and \(\underline{k}\), we have

blocks.alt: Three mutually perpendicular axes through the origin O: z upwards, y to the right and x coming towards the reader. Short arrows along them mark the unit vectors i on the x-axis, j on the y-axis and k on the z-axis.
blocks.caption: Figure: the unit vectors i, j and k along the coordinate axes (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why these values? \(\underline{i}\), \(\underline{j}\), \(\underline{k}\) are unit vectors, so each has magnitude \(1\).
In (a) a vector is multiplied with itself: the angle between a vector and itself is \(0^{\circ}\) and \(\cos 0^{\circ} = 1\), so the product is \(1 \times 1 \times 1 = 1\).
In (b) two different axes are used: the axes are perpendicular, the angle is \(90^{\circ}\) and \(\cos 90^{\circ} = 0\), so the product is \(0\).
The order does not matter: \(\underline{j} \cdot \underline{i}\), \(\underline{k} \cdot \underline{j}\) and \(\underline{i} \cdot \underline{k}\) are also \(0\) (see (c)).

blocks.caption: Our dot-product table of the unit vectors (row vector dot column vector)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Result (c) is the commutative property: the order of the two vectors in a dot product does not matter. The book measures the angle from \(\underline{v}\) back to \(\underline{u}\) as \(-\theta\); since cosine is an even function, \(\cos(-\theta) = \cos\theta\). Put simply, the angle between \(\underline{u}\) and \(\underline{v}\) is the same as the angle between \(\underline{v}\) and \(\underline{u}\), and \(|\underline{u}||\underline{v}| = |\underline{v}||\underline{u}|\) because ordinary numbers commute.
These results are used in 14.2.5 to prove the component formula \(\underline{u} \cdot \underline{v} = a_{1}a_{2} + b_{1}b_{2} + c_{1}c_{2}\): every product of two different unit vectors there becomes \(0\), and every product of a unit vector with itself becomes \(1\).

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text:
A quick use of the table (ours):
\[(2\underline{i}) \cdot (3\underline{i}) = 6(\underline{i} \cdot \underline{i}) = 6\]
\[(2\underline{i}) \cdot (5\underline{j}) = 10(\underline{i} \cdot \underline{j}) = 0\]
Numbers come out in front; then use the table.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Writing \(\underline{i} \cdot \underline{i} = 0\) or \(\underline{i} \cdot \underline{j} = 1\): it is the other way round. Same vector gives \(1\), different vectors give \(0\).
2. Writing \(\underline{i} \cdot \underline{j} = \underline{k}\). That is the cross product (14.3); a dot product is always a number.
